questions.concept: Predicted confirmation chance for waitlisted train tickets
questions.question: You're the PM for an Indian train-ticket booking app. Many users book waitlisted tickets for festival travel and then can't decide whether to also book a bus as a backup. Support gets many 'will my ticket confirm?' queries, and some users miss their trip because they waited too long to make a backup plan. What should you build first?
options: Faster automatic refunds for waitlisted tickets that don't confirm, so users get their money back without asking
A push alert sent each time the waitlist position moves, so users can follow their ticket's progress
A predicted chance of confirmation for each waitlisted ticket, based on how that train, class and date cleared in past years
A live chat with support agents who can check the current waitlist position for users on request
rationales: Refunds matter, but money back after the fact doesn't help someone who now has no way to travel.
More updates on the position still leave users guessing what the number means; frequent alerts add noise, not a decision.
Correct: it answers the question users actually have, early enough for them to book a backup if the odds are low.
Agents can only repeat the waitlist position, which is the same unclear number users already see; it adds cost without adding insight.
questions.explanation: The real pain is a decision made under uncertainty: should I book a backup now or wait? A waitlist position alone doesn't answer that, because how far a waitlist clears depends on the train, class and season. A predicted confirmation chance, shown at booking and updated later, lets users decide early enough to act. It also cuts the 'will it confirm?' support queries at their source.
questions.interview_tip: Strong candidates find the decision the user is stuck on, not just the information they lack. Turning raw data (a waitlist number) into a decision aid (a probability) is a pattern interviewers like to see.

questions.concept: Join-request screening questions for large community admins
questions.question: You're a PM on WhatsApp Communities. Admins of large neighbourhood communities (5,000+ members) say spammers and outsiders keep joining through shared invite links. Admins spend hours approving requests one by one with no idea who the people are. Which solution best fits the problem?
options: Let admins add short screening questions to join requests, with answers shown so they can approve in bulk
Cap communities at 1,000 members, so that admins receive far fewer join requests to review
Automatically approve anyone who already has at least one mutual contact inside the community
Remove invite links, so people can join only when an admin adds them directly by phone number
rationales: Correct: it adds the missing information and cuts review time, while keeping the easy invite link for genuine members.
Neighbourhood groups are large by nature; a cap breaks the use case instead of fixing the screening problem.
A mutual contact is a weak signal in a big neighbourhood, and spammers can easily get one; it removes admin control.
This stops spam but makes admins do even more manual work and makes it hard for real neighbours to join.
questions.explanation: The admin's problem has two parts: they lack information about who is asking, and reviewing takes too long. Screening questions (for example 'Which building do you live in?') give admins the context they need, and showing answers in a list lets them approve or reject many at once. The invite link keeps working for real neighbours, so growth isn't blocked.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers look for solutions that serve both sides: the admin's time and the genuine member's easy access. Naming what you are not willing to trade away (here, easy joining) shows mature judgement.

questions.concept: Step-free routing option for wheelchair and stroller users
questions.question: You're a PM on a maps app. Research shows wheelchair users and parents with strollers often give up on walking or transit routes midway because they hit stairs or a broken lift. What's the most valuable first thing to build?
options: A voice-guided mode with extra detailed spoken directions at every single turn
A step-free route option that avoids stairs and warns about known lift outages along the way
A city-wide accessibility map layer showing every ramp, lift and accessible toilet
A prompt asking users to rate each route's accessibility after they finish their trip
rationales: Detailed voice guidance helps blind or low-vision users, a different need; it doesn't remove stairs from the route.
Correct: it changes the route itself, which is where users are failing, and it helps many groups beyond wheelchair users.
A map layer gives information but leaves users to plan the route themselves; it doesn't stop the app suggesting stairs.
Ratings arrive slowly and only cover routes people already took; it doesn't help someone planning a trip today.
questions.explanation: Users fail at the routing step: the app sends them a way they physically can't use. A step-free routing option fixes that directly, and lift-outage warnings handle the most common surprise. It also helps a much wider group (travellers with luggage, older people), which strengthens the business case.
questions.interview_tip: Pointing out that an accessibility feature also helps a much larger group is a strong move in product sense rounds. It shows you can widen impact without losing focus on the core user.

questions.concept: Auto-downloading next episodes on Wi-Fi for commuters
questions.question: You're the PM for a video streaming app in India. Many users watch on their daily metro commute, where the network drops in tunnels. They often forget to download episodes beforehand. What's the best fix?
options: Preload a larger buffer of two minutes of video while streaming, to cover short network drops
Lower the default streaming quality for all users, so videos buffer less on weak mobile networks
Send a reminder every evening asking users to download episodes for the next day's commute
Automatically download the next episodes of shows they're watching when on home Wi-Fi, within a storage limit they set
rationales: A two-minute buffer doesn't cover long tunnel stretches and uses mobile data while streaming.
Lower quality helps on weak signal but not in tunnels with no signal at all, and it makes the experience worse for everyone.
A daily reminder adds a task and is easy to ignore; it still depends on users remembering to act.
Correct: it removes the step users forget, uses free Wi-Fi rather than mobile data, and respects storage limits.
questions.explanation: The problem is that users forget, so the fix should remove the need to remember. The app already knows what they're watching, so it can download the next episodes on Wi-Fi without any effort from them. A storage limit keeps them in control of their phone space.
questions.interview_tip: When the root cause is 'users forget', interviewers want to hear how you remove the step, not how you remind people. Using data the product already has is a sign of good product sense.

questions.concept: Offline viewing logged on reconnect undercounting recent engagement
questions.question: Two weeks after your streaming app launched offline downloads, the dashboard shows average daily watch time per user fell 12%. The drop is concentrated among users who downloaded episodes. Retention and subscription renewals are flat. What's the most likely explanation to check first?
options: Downloads lead users to binge less, so they now spend less total time watching the app
Offline viewing is logged only when the phone reconnects, so recent days undercount watch time
Users who download are lighter viewers to begin with, which pulls the average down
Downloaded video looks worse, so users stop watching episodes partway through
rationales: A real drop in viewing would usually show up in retention or renewals too; nothing suggests downloads reduce interest.
Correct: it explains why only downloaders are affected while retention and renewals stay flat; it's a logging delay, not a behaviour change.
Selection explains differences between groups, but these users' own watch time fell after launch, so it's a change over time, not a mix effect.
Downloads are usually the same or better quality, and this wouldn't explain why the drop appears so suddenly after launch.
questions.explanation: Offline plays can't be sent to the server until the device is back online, so recent days look low and fill in later. The clues fit: the drop is only among downloaders, and retention and renewals (which don't depend on those events) are flat. Check by comparing watch time by event time versus upload time, and by looking at whether older days were revised upward.
questions.interview_tip: In root-cause questions, interviewers reward checking the data pipeline before inventing a behaviour story. Saying 'which metrics did not move?' to narrow the cause is a strong signal.

questions.concept: RevPAR combines occupancy and average daily rate
questions.question: A hotel booking platform tracks RevPAR (revenue per available room) for its partner hotels. Which statement about RevPAR is correct?
options: It goes up whenever the hotel raises room prices, no matter what happens to occupancy
It measures profit per room after costs such as staff, cleaning and utilities are removed
It equals occupancy rate multiplied by average daily rate, so it reflects both price and how full the hotel is
It equals room revenue divided by the number of rooms actually sold on a given night
rationales: A price rise that drives occupancy down enough can lower RevPAR; that trade-off is exactly what it measures.
RevPAR is a revenue metric; profit per available room is a different metric (GOPPAR).
Correct: dividing by available rooms (not sold rooms) makes it capture both price and fill.
That's ADR (average daily rate), which ignores empty rooms.
questions.explanation: RevPAR is room revenue divided by all available rooms, which works out to occupancy × average daily rate (ADR). Because it combines both, a hotel can't look good just by charging more and leaving rooms empty, or by filling rooms at very low prices. It's the standard yield metric for supply with fixed capacity.
questions.interview_tip: Marketplace interviews often test whether you can pick a metric that balances price and volume. Explaining why the denominator is 'available' rather than 'sold' shows real understanding.

questions.concept: Rising search usage after a navigation redesign as a warning sign
questions.question: Your e-commerce app redesigned its category menu to make browsing simpler. After launch, the share of sessions that use search rose from 30% to 38%, and the team celebrates 'higher search engagement'. What's the best reading of this?
options: Higher search use is a positive engagement sign, which shows the menu redesign worked
It proves the menu redesign failed, so the team should roll it back immediately
Search use has nothing to do with the menu, so the rise must come from seasonal demand
It may mean users can't find items by browsing; check menu-to-product clicks and overall conversion
rationales: More activity isn't the goal; users switching to search could mean the redesign made browsing harder.
It's a warning sign, not proof; conversion might be fine, so check before rolling back.
The timing points to the redesign; dismissing it without checking ignores the most likely cause.
Correct: it treats the rise as a question and checks the outcome metrics that show whether users found what they wanted.
questions.explanation: Search and browse are two routes to the same goal. If people suddenly search more after a menu change, it may be because the menu stopped helping them. More use of a fallback route isn't a win by itself. Look at whether browse paths still lead to products and whether conversion held, before deciding.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like candidates who ask whether an 'engagement' metric going up is actually good. Linking a metric back to the user's goal is a key analytical skill.

questions.concept: Restating the baseline after a fake-account purge
questions.question: Your social app's trust team removed 4 million fake accounts in one week. Monthly active users (MAU) dropped 3% as a result, and leadership's quarterly MAU target is now at risk. What should you do?
options: Keep reporting the old MAU number, since the fake accounts were technically active on the app
Report it as a one-time cleanup, restate past MAU without the fake accounts, and reset the target on that base
Delay further cleanups until the next quarter starts, so this quarter's MAU target is not missed
Hide the cleanup week from all charts, so the trend line looks smooth and continuous
rationales: Counting fake accounts as users misleads leadership and advertisers about the real audience.
Correct: it keeps comparisons fair, protects trust in the metric, and doesn't penalise good safety work.
Delaying safety work to hit a number is Goodhart's law in action and lets harm continue.
Hiding the change makes the chart misleading; people need to know why the number moved.
questions.explanation: Fake accounts were never real users, so the old number overstated MAU. The honest fix is to restate history without them, so past and present are compared on the same basis, and to adjust the target. This keeps the metric trustworthy and avoids punishing the team that did the right thing.
questions.interview_tip: This tests integrity with data. A strong answer protects the metric's meaning over short-term targets and explains how to communicate the change.

questions.concept: Flicker effect in client-side web A/B tests
questions.question: You run a client-side A/B test on a website's checkout page: a script changes the button text after the page loads. The treatment shows a 2% drop in conversion, which surprises the team because the change was tiny. What's the most likely cause to check?
options: Client-side tests can't measure checkout conversion at all, so none of the test data can be trusted
Users briefly see the original page before the change applies, and that flicker and delay hurts conversion
The new button text is simply worse, so the team should accept the result and close the test
The test needs to run longer, because new button text always performs worse in its first weeks
rationales: Client-side tests can measure conversion; the issue is a specific bias, not that the data is useless.
Correct: the treatment includes a side effect (flicker and delay) that control doesn't, which can explain a surprising drop.
Possible, but a surprising result from a tiny change is a reason to check the setup before accepting it.
There's no rule that new text starts worse; running longer doesn't remove a bias built into the setup.
questions.explanation: In client-side tests, the treatment often loads extra script and swaps content after the page appears. Users may see the page 'jump' or wait longer, and that experience, not the new text, can drive the drop. Check page load timing by variant and look for a sample ratio mismatch. Server-side rendering of the variant avoids this problem.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers want to see that you question the test setup when a result is surprising. Naming implementation bias, not just statistics, sets strong candidates apart.

questions.concept: Judging a module test on page-level outcomes, not module clicks
questions.question: You test a new 'Frequently bought together' widget on product pages. In treatment, clicks on the widget are 40% higher. What should be the primary metric for the ship decision?
options: Time spent on the product page, since more exploring shows more shopping interest
Clicks on the widget, since the widget is the only part of the page that changed
Conversion or revenue per visitor across the whole session, not just widget clicks
Products viewed per session, since the widget is meant to show shoppers more items
rationales: More time on the page could mean confusion; it doesn't show buying.
A local metric can rise while the page as a whole does worse, for example if the widget distracts from 'Add to cart'.
Correct: it measures the actual goal and catches cases where the widget just moves clicks around.
Viewing more items isn't the goal; shoppers could view more and still buy less.
questions.explanation: Widget clicks can rise simply by taking clicks from other parts of the page, or by distracting people from buying what they came for. The business goal is more purchases, so judge the test on session-level conversion or revenue per visitor. Widget clicks are a useful supporting signal, not the decision metric.
questions.interview_tip: A classic trap is choosing the metric closest to the change. Strong candidates pick the outcome the business cares about and keep local metrics as diagnostics.

questions.concept: Annual printer-paper reams for a 2,000-person office
questions.question: Estimate how many reams of printer paper (500 sheets each) a 2,000-person office uses in a year. Assume about 5 printed pages per person per working day on average, single-sided, and 250 working days a year.
options: About 5,000 reams
About 2.5 million reams
About 500 reams
About 50,000 reams
rationales: Correct: 2,000 × 5 × 250 = 2.5 million pages, divided by 500 sheets per ream.
This is the number of pages, not reams; the last step of dividing by 500 was missed.
Too low by 10x; it's what you'd get with about half a page per person per day.
Too high by 10x; it would need about 50 pages per person every day.
questions.explanation: Pages per year = 2,000 people × 5 pages × 250 days = 2.5 million pages. Reams = 2.5 million ÷ 500 = 5,000 reams. The average of 5 pages blends people who print nothing with a few who print a lot. Always finish by converting to the unit asked for.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers watch whether you state assumptions clearly and check units at the end. Saying the average hides a skewed spread shows careful thinking.

questions.concept: Monthly backend API calls for a weather app
questions.question: A weather app has 10 million daily active users. Each user opens the app about 3 times a day, and each open makes 2 API calls (current weather and forecast). Roughly how many API calls does the backend serve per month (30 days)?
options: About 18 billion
About 1.8 billion
About 60 million
About 180 million
rationales: Too high by 10x; it would need about 20 opens per user per day.
Correct: 10M × 3 × 2 = 60M per day, × 30 days = 1.8 billion per month.
This is the daily number; the result wasn't multiplied by 30 days.
Too low by 10x; it's what you'd get with only 1 million daily users.
questions.explanation: Daily calls = 10 million users × 3 opens × 2 calls = 60 million per day. Monthly = 60 million × 30 = 1.8 billion. In a real plan you'd add background widget refreshes and retries, and use caching to cut calls for the same location, but the base estimate is about 1.8 billion.
questions.interview_tip: Technical estimation questions reward a clear chain from users to actions to calls. Mentioning what would raise or lower the number (widgets, caching) shows practical judgement.

questions.concept: Free education licences to build future enterprise demand
questions.question: A design software company gives free full licences to university students and teachers, even though these users would never pay enterprise prices. What's the main strategic reason?
options: It mainly stops student piracy, which is the biggest cause of lost enterprise licence sales
Student usage data is used to train the product's AI features, which is its main source of value
Free licences create a tax benefit that more than covers the cost of serving all these students
Students learn the tool and build habits, then push employers to buy it when they start working
rationales: Reducing piracy can be a side benefit, but students pirating wouldn't pay enterprise prices anyway.
Some products may use data, but this isn't the main reason, and many education terms limit such use.
There's no general tax benefit that justifies the programme; the value is in future customers.
Correct: it builds skills and loyalty that turn into enterprise demand once students join companies.
questions.explanation: This is seeding future demand. Professionals tend to stick with the tools they learned on, and new hires ask employers for them. Companies hiring graduates also prefer tools the talent pool already knows. The cost of serving students is small next to the future enterprise revenue it creates.
questions.interview_tip: Strategy rounds often ask why a company gives something away. Strong answers trace who pays later and how today's free users become tomorrow's buyers or influencers.

questions.concept: Negative cash conversion cycle in fast-growing retail
questions.question: A quick-commerce company in India collects payment from customers when they order, but pays suppliers 45 days later. Its inventory sells through in about 10 days. Why does this matter strategically?
options: Growth produces cash, because supplier credit pays for stock and operations before the bills are due
It lifts gross margin on every order, because paying later lowers the cost of the goods sold
It shows the company is profitable, because cash in the bank is larger than the bills it owes
It is only a risk, because suppliers can demand early payment at any time they choose
rationales: Correct: supplier credit funds the business, so growth releases cash rather than consuming it.
Payment timing doesn't change the price of goods, so gross margin is unchanged.
Holding cash isn't the same as profit; the business can still lose money on each order.
There's real risk if terms tighten or growth stops, but calling it 'only a risk' misses the funding advantage.
questions.explanation: This is a negative cash conversion cycle: about 10 days to sell stock minus 45 days to pay suppliers = about −35 days. The company holds customers' cash for weeks, so growing sales frees up cash to fund expansion. But it isn't profit, and it reverses if growth slows or suppliers shorten terms, which is a real risk to manage.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers at commerce companies like candidates who understand cash flow, not just margins. Separating cash from profit, and naming when the advantage reverses, is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Price as a quality signal for a new premium brand
questions.question: A new Indian D2C skincare brand priced its serum at ₹399, well below premium rivals at about ₹1,200. In interviews, shoppers say they doubt it works because it's 'too cheap'. Sales are weak despite good reviews. Which move fits the evidence best?
options: Reposition at a higher price with visible proof of quality, since low price is signalling low quality
Run heavy coupons and discounts to drive trial volume quickly in the first few months
Keep the price and increase ad spend on messages that highlight the low price point
Cut the price further to ₹299 to win more of the price-sensitive buyers in the market
rationales: Correct: it addresses the stated reason for weak sales, which is low trust caused by the low price.
Discounts lower the effective price even more and can cheapen the brand further.
Ads that stress the low price spread the very message that's putting shoppers off.
A lower price makes the 'too cheap to work' worry worse, not better.
questions.explanation: When shoppers can't judge quality before buying, they use price as a clue. Here the evidence is direct: shoppers say it's too cheap to trust. Raising the price alongside visible proof (ingredient strength, dermatologist testing, before-and-after results) matches how the category is judged. Cutting price further would deepen the doubt.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers want you to follow the customer evidence, even when it points to raising prices. Explaining when price acts as a quality signal shows strong pricing intuition.

questions.concept: Shared launch calendar to avoid overlapping launches
questions.question: Three teams at a food-delivery company plan to ship changes to the home screen in the same week, just before a festival. What's the main reason to coordinate through a shared launch calendar?
options: A shared calendar lets senior leaders personally approve every launch before it goes live
It makes sure each team gets an equal share of the marketing budget for its launch
Launching in the same week always causes technical conflicts between teams' code changes
Overlapping launches make results hard to attribute and can overwhelm users and support at once
rationales: The aim is coordination, not adding a senior approval step to every launch.
Marketing budget isn't the main reason; the calendar is about timing and clarity.
Code conflicts can happen, but they're managed in engineering; launch timing is about impact and measurement.
Correct: it protects measurement, user experience and operational load.
questions.explanation: When several changes hit the same surface at once, you can't tell which one moved the metrics, and users face a lot of change at the same time. Support and operations also get hit with everything together. A shared calendar lets teams space launches, agree on order, and avoid risky timing around peak events.
questions.interview_tip: Execution interviews test whether you think beyond your own team. Mentioning attribution and support load shows you understand how launches affect the wider company.

questions.concept: Five whys to go beyond 'human error' in a postmortem
questions.question: A postmortem for a payment outage says: 'Root cause: an engineer deployed a bad config.' What's the best next step to improve the postmortem?
options: Keep asking why a bad config could reach production, until you find a gap in process or tools you can fix
Close the postmortem now, since the cause is known and the config has already been fixed
Require that engineer to get a manager's approval before making any future deployments
Add the incident to the team's risk register and plan to review it again next quarter
rationales: Correct: it finds the system gaps that let one mistake cause an outage, which is what prevents repeats.
Fixing the config solves this incident only; the conditions that allowed it remain.
Blaming one person adds friction and doesn't stop anyone else making the same mistake.
Logging and waiting doesn't produce action; postmortems should create concrete fixes with owners.
questions.explanation: 'Someone made a mistake' is where the analysis should start, not end. Asking why repeatedly (why wasn't the config validated? why did it go to all servers at once? why didn't alerts fire sooner?) leads to fixes like config checks, staged rollouts and better alerts. Those prevent the next person making the same mistake.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers listen for blameless thinking. Showing you look for system fixes rather than people to blame is a strong signal for both execution and leadership.

questions.concept: Quantifying tech debt cost to win prioritisation
questions.question: Your engineering lead wants a quarter to clean up an old checkout service, but leadership keeps choosing new features instead. What's the most effective way to make the case?
options: Quietly pause new feature work and do the clean-up without asking for approval
Explain that clean code is an engineering best practice the company should always follow
Quantify the debt's cost: incidents, on-call hours, and how much it slows every checkout change
Ask for 20% of capacity for tech debt every sprint, without naming what it will fix
rationales: Going around the decision damages trust and leaves features unexpectedly late.
Best-practice arguments rarely beat concrete business value in prioritisation discussions.
Correct: it puts tech debt in the same terms as features, so leadership can compare them fairly.
A standing allowance can help, but without a clear purpose it's easy to cut and hard to defend.
questions.explanation: Leaders compare options in terms of impact. Tech debt competes better when its cost is visible: outages, lost orders, engineer time spent firefighting, and how many weeks it adds to each feature. Framing the clean-up as 'features ship X% faster afterwards' turns it into a business choice leaders can weigh fairly.
questions.interview_tip: This comes up as 'how do you balance tech debt and features?'. Strong answers translate engineering work into business impact and show you partner with engineering rather than overrule it.

questions.concept: Raising that your own OKR target was set too low
questions.question: Four weeks into the quarter, your team has already hit its main OKR. The target was set low because last quarter's data was incomplete. Your manager's own review depends partly on your team's results. What do you do?
options: Ask the team to slow down on that goal, so the results look steady across the quarter
Tell your manager the target was mis-set, propose a higher one based on current data, and keep pushing
Keep the target as it is and present the over-achievement at quarter end as a big win
Keep the target quietly and move the team onto other work for the rest of the quarter
rationales: Slowing down on purpose to manage appearances is gaming the metric and hurts the business.
Correct: it's honest, keeps goals meaningful and shows ownership of results over looking good.
Claiming a big win on a mis-set target misleads leadership and erodes trust when it comes out.
Quietly coasting wastes the chance for more impact and hides that the goal was wrong.
questions.explanation: A target set from incomplete data doesn't reflect what the team can achieve. Raising it openly keeps goals meaningful and builds trust with leadership. It also keeps the team focused on real impact. A good answer would add that you share the reasons and make it easy for your manager to explain the change upward.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon-style rounds test whether you hold yourself to a high bar when no one is forcing you. Volunteering a harder target is a strong signal of ownership and integrity.

questions.concept: Disclosing a personal conflict of interest in vendor selection
questions.question: You're leading the selection of a customer-support AI vendor. One shortlisted vendor was co-founded by your close friend, and they also score best on your evaluation. Your VP wants your recommendation tomorrow. What's the best approach?
options: Recommend the vendor, since they won fairly on the scoring and the friendship didn't affect it
Remove the vendor from the shortlist, to avoid any appearance of bias in the decision
Disclose the relationship now, share your scoring openly, and ask someone else to review or decide
Recommend the second-best vendor, so that nobody can question your motives later
rationales: You may be unbiased, but hiding the relationship risks trust and may break company policy.
Dropping the strongest option to avoid appearances costs the company a better choice.
Correct: transparency plus an independent check keeps the decision both fair and trusted.
Picking a worse vendor on purpose is a bad business decision made to protect yourself.
questions.explanation: Even if your scoring is fair, others can't see that without knowing the relationship. Disclosing early and letting someone independent check the process protects you, the company and the vendor. Removing the best option to look neutral hurts the business; staying silent risks trust if it surfaces later.
questions.interview_tip: Integrity questions reward disclosure plus a process that still lets the best option win. Showing you protect both fairness and outcomes is what interviewers listen for.

questions.concept: Supporting an engineer who wants to move into product management
questions.question: A strong engineer on your team tells you they want to move into product management. The team needs their engineering skills for a critical launch next quarter. What's the best response?
options: Tell them to wait until after the launch, and revisit the idea at next year's performance review
Back the goal: give them scoped PM work like a spec or user interviews, and plan timing with their manager
Advise them that engineers usually make weak PMs, so staying in their current role is better
Move them into PM work straight away, and find a replacement engineer for the launch later
rationales: Pushing it off a year without any steps signals you don't care, and you may lose them entirely.
Correct: it supports their growth now while protecting the launch through a planned transition.
This is untrue and discouraging; many strong PMs come from engineering.
Moving them immediately puts the critical launch at risk and skips their manager.
questions.explanation: Supporting growth keeps strong people engaged, and giving them small PM tasks lets them test the fit with low risk. Working with their engineering manager on timing protects the launch. A plan with both near-term steps and a realistic transition date respects the person and the team's commitments.
questions.interview_tip: Leadership questions often test whether you develop people, not just ship. Balancing someone's growth with team commitments shows maturity.

questions.concept: Rough word-to-token conversion for English text
questions.question: You're estimating LLM costs for an English-language feature. Users send about 750 words per request. Roughly how many input tokens is that?
options: About 200 tokens
About 3,000 tokens
About 1,000 tokens
About 750 tokens
rationales: Far too low; tokens are usually smaller than words, not larger.
Too high; it assumes about four tokens per word, roughly 3x the usual English ratio.
Correct: about 0.75 words per token means 750 words is roughly 1,000 tokens.
This assumes one token per word, but many words split into more than one token.
questions.explanation: For English, a common rule of thumb is about 0.75 words per token, or about 4 characters per token. So 750 words is roughly 1,000 tokens. Exact counts vary by tokenizer, and other languages often use many more tokens per word, so check with the provider's tokenizer before final pricing.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews often include quick cost maths. Knowing the words-to-tokens rule, and that it changes by language, shows you can size costs on the spot.

questions.concept: LLM pre-labelling with human-verified agreement for eval sets
questions.question: Your team needs 20,000 labelled support tickets to evaluate a new intent classifier. Human labelling alone would take 6 weeks. What's the most sensible approach?
options: Have an LLM pre-label tickets, check its agreement against a human-labelled sample, and send unsure cases to humans
Use the LLM's labels as ground truth for every ticket, since LLMs are very accurate at classifying text
Wait the full six weeks for human labels, since only human labels can ever be trusted for evaluation
Hand-label only 200 tickets and skip the rest, since a small sample is always enough for evaluation
rationales: Correct: it's fast, measures the LLM's label quality, and uses humans where they add the most value.
Without checking, you don't know the error rate, and the eval may share the same blind spots as the model.
Human labels aren't the only option, and a six-week delay is costly when a checked hybrid works.
200 tickets is too few to measure performance on each intent, especially rare ones.
questions.explanation: LLMs can label quickly, but you need to know how often they agree with careful human labels before trusting them. A human-labelled sample measures that agreement, and routing low-confidence or disputed cases to humans focuses expert time where it matters. This gets most of the speed while keeping label quality known.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like answers that balance speed and quality with a way to measure the trade-off. Saying 'measure agreement on a sample first' is a strong signal.

questions.concept: Live tool calls for fast-changing values instead of indexed retrieval
questions.question: An airline's AI assistant answers questions about fares and seat availability using RAG over an index that updates nightly. Users complain that it quotes fares that no longer exist. What's the best fix?
options: Fine-tune the model on recent fare data, so it learns the current prices for each route
Get fares and seats from a live API tool call when answering, and keep RAG for policies and FAQs
Re-index the fare data every hour, so the fares that the assistant retrieves are much fresher
Add a disclaimer telling users that the fares shown in answers may have changed since
rationales: Fine-tuning bakes in prices that go out of date immediately and is the slowest way to update facts.
Correct: it uses the right method for each kind of data, giving current prices and stable policy answers.
Hourly updates are still stale for fares that change minute to minute, and re-indexing costs more.
A disclaimer admits the problem without fixing it, and users still get wrong prices.
questions.explanation: Fares and seats change by the minute, so any index will go stale. A live tool call fetches the current value at the moment of answering, while RAG stays the right fit for slower-changing content like baggage rules. Choose how to get data based on how quickly it changes.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers probe whether you can match the architecture to the data. Explaining 'live lookup for volatile data, retrieval for stable documents' shows technical judgement.

questions.concept: Claim-level vs response-level hallucination measurement
questions.question: Your team reports that an AI research summariser has a '4% hallucination rate'. You learn it's the share of summaries reviewers rated 'mostly made up'. Summaries average 12 factual claims. What's the main problem with this metric?
options: Reviewer ratings are subjective, so only automatic scores like ROUGE should be used here
The sample is the main issue; with more summaries rated, the 4% figure becomes reliable
4% is too high for any launch, so the feature should not ship until it reaches zero
It misses summaries with one or two false claims; measure the share of claims that aren't supported
rationales: ROUGE measures word overlap, not whether claims are true, so it's worse for this purpose.
More data makes a badly defined metric more precise, but it's still measuring the wrong thing.
Zero is rarely realistic; the issue is that this number doesn't measure the right thing.
Correct: the metric's unit is too coarse and hides the single false claims that users actually trip over.
questions.explanation: Rating whole summaries as 'mostly made up' only catches the worst cases. A summary with 11 true claims and one false one counts as fine, even though that one error could mislead a user. Checking each claim against the source gives a truer error rate and shows which kinds of claims fail.
questions.interview_tip: Strong AI PMs question how a quality metric is defined before trusting the number. Choosing the right unit of measurement (claim, not response) is a high-signal answer.

questions.concept: Adverse selection in flat-rate unlimited AI plans
questions.question: You launched an 'unlimited' AI image-generation plan at a flat ₹999/month, priced from beta users' average usage. Three months later the plan loses money: average usage per subscriber is 3x the beta average. Subscribers who were also in the beta use about the same as before. What's the most likely cause?
options: The price was too low for the market, where users actually expect to pay a lot more
Beta users underused the product because it was new, and everyone's usage has since grown
Inference costs rose across the industry, so every image now costs much more to generate
Heavy users chose the unlimited plan most, so subscribers aren't like the average beta user
rationales: Price level may need to change, but this doesn't explain why usage per subscriber is 3x higher.
Former beta users use about the same, so usage hasn't grown across the board.
Nothing points to higher costs; the problem is higher usage per subscriber, and model prices generally fall.
Correct: the buyers selected themselves toward heavy use, so the average used for pricing was the wrong one.
questions.explanation: This is adverse selection: an unlimited plan is most attractive to the people who use the most. Pricing from the average of all beta users ignores that the plan's buyers will be heavier than average. Former beta users haven't changed, so the gap comes from who signed up. Fixes include fair-use limits, tiered plans, or pricing based on likely buyers' usage.
questions.interview_tip: AI pricing questions often hinge on who chooses each plan. Spotting self-selection and proposing fair-use limits or tiers shows strong business sense.

questions.concept: Replication is not a backup
questions.question: Your startup's database has a live replica in another region, so the team says 'we don't need backups'. Why is this risky?
options: Cloud providers delete replicas after 30 days unless a separate backup also exists for them
Replicas can't serve any reads, so they don't help at all if the main database goes down
An accidental delete or bad migration is copied to the replica too, so the old data can't be recovered
Replicas are always several hours behind, so they lose the most recent data during any failure
rationales: There's no such general rule; replicas stay as long as you keep them running.
Replicas can usually serve reads and can be promoted if the main database fails.
Correct: replication copies mistakes, so only backups let you go back to a good state.
Replica lag is usually seconds, not hours; the bigger risk is that it copies errors.
questions.explanation: Replication copies every change, including mistakes. If someone deletes a table or a migration corrupts data, the replica does the same within seconds. Backups (and point-in-time recovery) let you restore to before the mistake. Replicas protect against a server or region failing; backups protect against bad changes.
questions.interview_tip: Technical rounds check whether you know what each safeguard protects against. Separating 'failure of hardware' from 'bad data changes' shows sound fluency.

questions.concept: Authenticator-app TOTP vs SMS OTP security
questions.question: A fintech app uses SMS one-time passwords for login. The security team recommends adding authenticator-app codes (TOTP) as an option. What's the main security benefit?
options: Authenticator codes fully stop phishing, because they can't be typed into fake websites
It removes the need for a password or any other factor when users log in to the app
Codes never expire, so users don't get locked out if they are slow to type them in
Codes are generated on the user's device, so SIM-swap and SMS interception attacks can't steal them
rationales: Users can still type a TOTP code into a fake site, so it doesn't fully stop phishing.
TOTP is usually a second factor alongside a password, not a replacement for all factors.
TOTP codes expire quickly, usually every 30 seconds; that's part of their security.
Correct: removing the phone network from the flow blocks SIM-swap and interception attacks.
questions.explanation: SMS codes travel over the phone network, so attackers who take over a phone number (SIM swap) or intercept messages can receive them. TOTP codes are created on the device from a shared secret and never sent over SMS. They can still be phished on a fake site, which is why passkeys are stronger still.
questions.interview_tip: PMs on fintech or identity teams get asked about login security trade-offs. Knowing what each method does and doesn't protect against shows credible technical depth.

questions.concept: Gift subscriptions judged by recipient conversion to paid
questions.question: A language-learning app is launching gift subscriptions before the holiday season. What should be the main success metric for gifting as a growth channel?
options: Share of gift recipients who activate and then renew as paying users after the gift ends
Revenue from gift purchases compared with revenue from regular subscriptions
Number of gift buyers who share their gift purchase on social media channels
Number of gift subscriptions sold during the holiday season compared with last year
rationales: Correct: it measures whether gifting creates new lasting customers, which is the growth purpose.
Gift revenue is one-off and may just shift spending from existing buyers.
Sharing is a weak proxy; it doesn't show that anyone new became a paying user.
Sales count shows demand for gifts but not whether recipients ever use or keep the product.
questions.explanation: Gift sales bring in one-off revenue, but the growth value comes from recipients who become long-term paying users. Many gifts go unused, so tracking activation and conversion when the gift period ends shows whether the channel creates new customers. Gift sales count is a useful early number but not the main goal.
questions.interview_tip: Growth interviews test whether you measure the loop, not just the first step. Following the user past the gift to renewal shows clear growth thinking.

questions.concept: Verifying vendor price-performance claims with your own evals (Microsoft MAI, Nov 2026)
questions.question: At Microsoft Ignite on 17 November 2026, Microsoft said its new MAI Code 2 Flash model matches Claude Haiku 5.5 'at 20% of the price', with availability in GitHub Copilot and a limited preview in Microsoft Foundry. You run a high-volume code-review feature on Haiku. What's the best first step?
options: Run your own eval set on your tasks, comparing quality, latency and total cost per task, then shift traffic gradually
Switch all traffic to the new model right away, since the 80% saving is too large to wait on
Ignore the claim entirely, since vendor benchmark numbers are only marketing and can't be tested
Wait for general availability, then switch over completely if other companies report good results
rationales: Correct: it tests the claim on your actual workload and limits risk with a gradual switch.
A big saving is worth testing, but switching blind risks quality drops in a high-volume feature.
Vendor claims can be tested cheaply on your own data; ignoring an 80% potential saving is a missed opportunity.
Other companies' workloads differ from yours, and waiting delays a saving you could verify now.
questions.explanation: Vendor comparisons use the vendor's chosen benchmarks, and coverage of the launch noted they weren't independently verified. Even the same article gave inconsistent figures for a sibling model. A model that matches on a benchmark can still do worse on your code, languages or prompts. Your own eval, plus a gradual rollout with monitoring, tells you whether the saving holds for your users.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews often ask how you'd react to a cheaper model launch. A strong answer treats it as a hypothesis to test with evals and a staged rollout, not as a decision already made.
